title: From Canonical to Tunable Phase Diagrams in Open Quantum Long-Range Systems
abstract: We investigate the dissipative dynamics of a generalized Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) model coupled to a thermal environment. In this generalized model, in addition to the conventional quadratic interaction, one considers quartic interactions between spin-$1/2$'s coupled all-to-all and evolving in presence of a transverse field. Employing the usual linear Lindblad master equation with thermally-balanced jump processes, we derive magnetisation evolution equations, and demonstrate that the corresponding stationary solution reproduces the canonical equilibrium phase diagram of the model. We then extend our analysis to a nonlinear Lindblad equation that incorporates imperfect quantum-jump processes in terms of jump-retention parameters. Here, remarkably, the system relaxes to a genuine nonequilibrium stationary state whose properties differ qualitatively from those obtained in the linear case. The jump-retention parameters provide tunable knobs that shift the phase boundaries and even modify the nature of the phase transitions with respect to the linear case. Our exact results establish a direct connection between dissipative relaxation dynamics and stationary-state behavior, while identifying controlled quantum-jump retention as a mechanism for engineering nonequilibrium phases in long-range interacting open quantum systems.
summary: This paper analyzes the dynamics of an open quantum spin system, showing that moving beyond ideal Lindblad evolution by incorporating imperfect quantum jumps allows for profound control over its steady state. By tuning these 'jump-retention' parameters, researchers can engineer entirely new nonequilibrium phase diagrams, demonstrating a powerful mechanism for controlling collective quantum behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates how controlled dissipation, implemented via imperfect quantum jumps, can fundamentally alter the stationary state of an open quantum system compared to its canonical thermal equilibrium.
main_result: The analysis demonstrates that by tuning jump-retention parameters, one can engineer genuine nonequilibrium stationary states (NESS) whose phase transition boundaries and nature differ qualitatively from the standard linear Lindblad case.
method: The authors employ mean-field approximations applied to the Lindblad master equation, extending it to a nonlinear form incorporating imperfect quantum jumps. Phase transitions are analyzed by solving self-consistency equations for the magnetization order parameter.
model_or_system: The system is a generalized Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) model of interacting spin-1/2 particles coupled to a thermal environment. The dynamics are governed by both linear and nonlinear Lindblad master equations, incorporating quartic interactions and transverse fields.
key_observables: Magnetization components ($\langle m_x angle, \langle m_y angle, \langle m_z angle$), the stationary state expectation value $\langle m_z angle_{ss}$, and coefficients determining transition order ($A, B$).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), transverse field strength ($h$), interaction strengths ($J, K$), and crucially, the jump-retention parameters ($\eta_1, \eta_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mean-field approximations in the thermodynamic limit and extends the standard Markovian Lindblad framework to include imperfect quantum jumps.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams in parameter space (e.g., $(h, K)$) showing regions of continuous vs. first-order transitions controlled by jump parameters, and plots demonstrating how $\langle m_z angle_{ss}$ changes across tricritical points.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing the standard linear Lindblad dynamics (reproducing equilibrium phase diagrams) to introducing a nonlinear extension via imperfect jumps. The core analysis then focuses on mapping out the parameter space where these controlled dissipative mechanisms allow for engineering novel, nonequilibrium stationary states with tunable critical behavior.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a concrete theoretical framework for using engineered dissipation (non-Markovian or non-ideal jump processes) to control and stabilize quantum phases inaccessible under standard thermal equilibrium assumptions.
